title: Five Questions with Mississippi Voting Rights Lawyer Amir Badat - Civil Discourse with Joyce Vance
text:
Five Questions with Mississippi Voting Rights Lawyer Amir Badat 
 Civil Discourse with Joyce Vance 
 Subscribe Sign in Five Questions with Mississippi Voting Rights Lawyer Amir Badat
 Nov 14, 2026 ∙ Paid 163 6 42 Share The election in Mississippi was not supposed to be a nail-biter. But it turned into one. 
 When all hell broke loose after early election results showed the Democrat in the Senate race, Scott Colom, ahead by just a few hundred votes, Amir Badat did not have to get on a plane or hop in a car to get to Mississippi. That’s because Amir lives there. He’s a voting rights expert who understands the ins and outs of Mississippi’s electoral system, voting laws, and local politics. And he was there, boots on the ground, as the count began to unfold.
 Amir wasn’t surprised when the press started reporting about the incredible jump in the number of people who had to vote “affidavit ballots” (you might call them provisional in your state) after Mississippi’s Secretary of State ordered the use of commercial data from credit agency Experian to determine which voters should be moved to inactive status. Amir had been flagging the problems with this approach all along. Although Colom won, narrowly, there are lingering issues involving Mississippi voters’ ability to cast a ballot and even to register and stay registered to vote. And those problems could be coming to, or already in, a state near you as a push to use commercial data to assess voter status continues to unfold.
 So there’s no one better to catch us up on how the vote count unfolded, the questionable data Mississippi used to knock voters out of active status, and what that could mean beyond Mississippi. The state has more elections coming next year, which also raises an interesting question: Was this election just a one-off, or is Mississippi trending blue, or at least purple? 
 Amir is a voting Rights Attorney and political strategist at Fair Fight Action. We are incredibly fortunate to have him with us tonight! I note that the timestamp on his email to me with his responses to these questions was 2 a.m. That tells you what kind of week he’s had. I’m grateful he’s made time to bring us up to date. 
 “Five Questions” is a Friday feature for paid subscribers, built around the conversations that don’t fit into a news cycle driven by headlines and hot takes. It’s a chance to spend time with the people shaping the law, politics, and democracy—and to ask the questions that matter most, not just the ones everyone else is asking. Keeping the daily legal analysis free is important to me. These Friday conversations give me a chance to thank paid subscribers for their help ensuring that Civil Discourse remains available to everyone who wants to follow the law beyond the day’s headlines and offer some deeper insight. Whether you’re a paid subscriber or a free subscriber, I’m grateful you’re here.
